sections.html:
A Plainfield owner can list through an agent, handle the sale personally, or hand the house to a buyer paying cash who accepts it unrepaired. Price, effort and speed pull in different directions, so start from the shape the house is in and the date you must be out.

Plainfield has grown quickly, from about 4,500 residents in 1990 to 50,043 now, so a newer subdivision house competes against many near-identical neighbors, while a home near the old downtown draws a different crowd. Rank these goals before you pick:

  • Getting the highest possible price, which usually means repairs, staging and showings.
  • Closing on your own schedule, which often favors a direct sale with no financing contingency.
  • Avoiding repairs on a house with deferred maintenance, storm damage or a failing system.
  • Handling an inherited house, a divorce sale or a move that cannot wait for a long listing period.

Because a cash purchase skips the lender's appraisal, one common cause of failed contracts disappears. Even so, set any offer next to what a listing might realistically bring, and have the terms put in writing before you sign anything.

Owners live in 88.0 percent of Plainfield homes, and much of the housing is under thirty years old, so buyers will ask about roof age, HVAC replacement dates and any homeowner association rules.

A median hides a wide spread. A downtown cottage and a newer four-bedroom on a cul-de-sac sit in different price brackets, so treat these numbers as background and not as an offer on your own address.

Plainfield sits in northwestern Will County, and the village limits reach west into Kendall County. Some addresses are recorded, assessed and taxed through Kendall County offices even though the mailing address says Plainfield. Check the parcel record before you assume which county handles your deed.

Whichever county contains the parcel handles the recording: Will County for most of the village, Kendall County for the western part. Each county sets its own fees and document standards, so ask that recorder's office for the current schedule.

The land here is flat, and the DuPage River runs through the village center. Ask your title company whether any part of your lot touches a mapped flood area, because that affects insurance and a buyer's lender.

sections.h2: Which school district is your house in?
sections.html:
Most of the village falls inside Plainfield Community Consolidated School District 202, but not every Plainfield address does. Parts of the village are served by Oswego Community Unit School District 308 and Indian Prairie Community Unit School District 204, and in Kendall County most of the Plainfield land lies in the Oswego district.

Buyers often search by district first, so confirm yours before you write a listing. If you have children in school and need to move quickly, say so up front to whoever you sell to. A buyer who knows your timeline can often accommodate a rent-back period, which lets you finish a school year before handing over keys.

The Village of Plainfield runs its building permit process through an online permitting and licensing portal, and its Building and Code Enforcement department takes complaints by phone, email or an online form. If you have open work, an unfinished deck or a basement finished without a permit, resolve it before a buyer's inspector finds it.

The village also has a Preservation Commission and a historic preservation ordinance. If your house is in the older core around Lockport Street, ask the village planning staff whether exterior changes need review.

A boom of new subdivisions followed the 1990 tornado, which damaged or destroyed more than 1,100 homes, so many Plainfield houses share a similar age and construction era. Buyers of those homes often ask about roof age, siding and the sump pump.

sections.h2: The Illinois transfer declaration and stamps
sections.html:
Illinois law requires a transfer declaration. Under 35 ILCS 200/31-25, it must be presented with the deed, or within three business days after the transfer, whichever is earlier, and signed by at least one seller and one buyer or their attorneys or agents. The form asks for the property's value, parcel number, legal description, deed date and type, street address, type of improvement, lot size, any homestead exemptions on the latest tax bill, and whether the transfer is between related parties.

A deed will not be accepted for recording without that declaration, unless an exemption applies under section 31-45. The county collects state transfer tax through revenue stamps at 50¢ for each $500 of value, rounding up for any fraction, under section 31-15. Whoever runs your closing normally prepares both the declaration and the stamps.

sections.h2: What must a Plainfield seller disclose?
sections.html:
A short list of papers makes a Plainfield closing smoother: the deed, the latest tax bill showing any homestead exemption, the parcel number, repair invoices, and a signed disclosure report. Your title company will ask for the parcel number first, since it decides which county handles recording. If the house is an inherited one, add the estate paperwork to that pile, and tell your closing agent early who has the authority to sign for the sellers, so the signature page is not a surprise at the table.

Illinois sellers of residential property must fill in every item of the state disclosure report and hand it to the buyer before a contract is signed (765 ILCS 77/20).

Section 25 of the same act says a seller must disclose material defects the seller actually knows about, and is not required to hire anyone to investigate. A seller is not liable for an error if the seller did not know of it, believed a defect had been fixed, or relied on information from a public agency or a qualified professional. Take your time filling out the report, and keep copies, including any repair invoices that support what you wrote.

  • List known roof, foundation, basement water and drainage problems.
  • Note any past repairs and who did them.
  • Describe what you know about nearby issues such as construction, traffic or highway noise.

faqs.q: Must a Plainfield seller fix things before selling?
faqs.a: No. An as-is sale is allowed, whether to a cash buyer or on the open market, but the Illinois disclosure report still has to list defects you know about. A buyer will price the unrepaired items into the offer.

faqs.q: Which county records my Plainfield deed, Will or Kendall?
faqs.a: It depends on where the parcel sits. Most of the village is in Will County and the western edge is in Kendall County. Look at the parcel number on your tax bill or ask your title company, then contact that county's recorder for fees and format rules.

faqs.q: Does Plainfield have a historic district that limits what I can change?
faqs.a: The village has a Preservation Commission and a historic preservation ordinance. Whether your house is covered depends on its location and designation, so ask village planning staff before you list a house in the older downtown area.

faqs.q: What paperwork do I sign at a Plainfield closing besides the deed?
faqs.a: You will sign the Illinois transfer declaration along with the deed, plus a closing statement and the title company's affidavits. The disclosure report should already have gone to the buyer before the contract was signed.

faqs.q: How is the state transfer tax collected in Plainfield?
faqs.a: The county collects it through revenue stamps at 50¢ for each $500 of value, rounding up for any fraction. Whoever runs your closing normally prepares the stamps along with the declaration.
